hints.hint: For puzzles where agents announce ignorance, first write down exactly what each agent knows. If the setup leaves ambiguous which of two quantities was revealed, that ambiguity is part of every agent's uncertainty: do not case-split externally, assume one reading, and restart. An agent holding x who sees N must keep every partner value legal under either reading (sum/product reveal: N-x and N/x when each is a valid natural number). "I do not know" means at least two partner values survive, which constrains that agent's own number. Apply announcements in order, filtering the set left by the previous one. Verify at the end: your candidate makes both announcements true and no rival candidate does. Track eliminations once and move forward instead of relitigating; looping exhausts your budget before you answer.

Whenever an equation equates two n-th powers of linear expressions in z, take moduli before hunting roots. FIRST MOVE: from (z-a)^n = c(z-b)^n, divide by (z-b)^n to get ((z-a)/(z-b))^n = c, then take moduli: |z-a| = k|z-b|. TRAP: k is the n-th ROOT of |c|, not |c| raised to the n-th power; verify k^n = |c| first, since a wrong k gives a self-consistent but wrong circle. Then set z = x+iy, square, collect the x^2+y^2 terms, divide by their coefficient, complete the square, read off center and radius (k=1 gives a line). Check numerically against the ORIGINAL equation, never your derived one: build one explicit root and measure its distance to your center. Report exactly one value, then stop.

Covered area = sum of areas minus overlap, so minimize overlap. Fix coordinates once, with the shared point at the origin, and never re-derive that setup. Key pruning: only the two edges meeting at the shared point can cut the small square; the far edges are too distant to matter, so the overlap is a right-angle wedge. Never conclude the small square is wholly covered; the wedge apex sits at its center. Then be numeric, not qualitative: for one angle, find where the two rays exit the square, list the polygon vertices in order, and shoelace it. Repeat for a second angle. If the two values agree, the overlap is angle-independent; never argue minimality in prose. Trust the shoelace numbers over any closed-form guess, never restart, and once a number is in hand do not re-derive it or write a formatted solution: state that one value in one short line and stop.

Several hidden degree-n polynomials must jointly hit prescribed values at consecutive integers. Two traps: do NOT difference one polynomial and conclude impossibility, and do NOT assume each polynomial is used once.

Method: write the prescribed value as a function of the INPUT, not the position; for an arithmetic progression over consecutive inputs the target is affine, L(x)=px+q. Fix one polynomial P and set g=P-L. Every input assigned to P is a root of g. Compare degrees to show g is not identically zero, so g has at most n roots; that caps how many inputs any single polynomial can serve. Multiply/sum that cap over the family for the upper bound, then exhibit a construction giving each polynomial a disjoint block of inputs where it interpolates L. Report one exact integer.

When unknown points on a fixed curve y=g(x) are tied by a known displacement (u,v), reduce to ONE unknown: let the free vertex be (t, g(t)) and its partner (t+u, g(t)+v), then solve the single scalar equation g(t+u) = g(t) + v.

For a logarithmic curve, convert that additive offset to a multiplicative one BEFORE cross-multiplying: log_c(B) - log_c(A) = v means B/A = c^v. Flipping the direction or sign of that power is the dominant failure mode.

If you hit an impossible identity or a negative discriminant, you flipped the offset: recheck only that conversion line. Do not conclude the configuration is impossible, and do not restart from scratch.

Discard roots that reproduce a given vertex (degenerate). Finish with the shoelace determinant in cyclic order.

Describe a configuration by the ordered contents of the truck, gate, and shed rather than by informal move sequences. Legal moves form a small state graph; at each state, attach the actual transition probability, noting that it changes when only one move is available. Each stack is last-in-first-out, so translate the asked-about position into a timing claim: whatever is deposited first sits at the bottom. Then trace only the move sequences that realize that event, multiplying 1/2 per step where two moves were genuinely available, and add those path probabilities. Do not substitute a symmetry claim that each item is equally likely to occupy each position; the induced distribution over orders is not uniform. Report exactly one value per part, then stop.

Interpret the unknowns as weights of a functional L(f) = sum of weight_i times f(node_i) over distinct nodes. The vanishing conditions say L kills a consecutive block of monomials; the last fixes L on one more. Note which monomial is NOT prescribed (often the constant) and never use it. First move: build ONE explicit product polynomial vanishing at every node but the target one and expanding only in prescribed monomials; evaluate L on it twice - by linearity, and as the target weight times its value at that node. Solve that one equation. Do not invert the system, re-index, or test a small analogue. Reduce the product of node differences to a factorial, commit to one value, and stop reasoning.

Let H be the total number of houses. The equal-street layout constrains H arithmetically, and integer stage costs per house mean H must divide every listed stage total. Determine the admissible common divisors using the intended maximum-feasible-count interpretation. Add all construction costs before dividing by H, apply the stated markup multiplicatively, and check integrality and units.

When the constraint is a commuting identity like p(q(x)) = q(p(x)) with unknown coefficients, do not expand the composition: its degree is the product of the degrees, and drowning in that algebra is the main way these problems are lost. Instead posit the affine link q = -p + b and fix b from the given point values; do not spend budget on the q = p + constant branch, since a nonzero constant shift cannot commute. The identity then collapses to p(-p+b) = -p(p)+b; match the top couple of coefficients to pin p. Expect one leftover free coefficient; verify the requested outputs do not depend on it, then set it to something convenient. Evaluate each requested output through q = -p + b at the needed point rather than re-expanding q term by term - that re-expansion is where sign slips kill otherwise correct work. Recheck the given values once, then report one result and stop.

First move: for the two smallest sizes, write positions 0..N-1 as an explicit list and rewrite the entire list after each stage k=0,1,...,n-1 in order; that is one operation. After every stage the list must still contain each label exactly once; if two labels land in one slot your bookkeeping is broken, so redo that stage by physically swapping the two blocks. Reapply the whole operation and track the orbit of a single label until it repeats. That cycle length is your candidate order. Trap: the stages overlap, so the composite is not a product of disjoint swaps and usually is not its own inverse; never assert order 2, and never reuse a stage-level shortcut, unless your trace confirms it. If a formula and a trace disagree, trust the trace. Once two sizes agree, stop exploring, never restart the analysis, and report exactly one closed form in n, then stop.
